title: Why Nice People Don’t Get Promoted at Work
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Colette Molteni, writing from her experience in Lean Six Sigma and analytics, describes a highly capable colleague who was steered away from business-critical projects after being labeled one of the sweetest people to work with. She argues that vague feedback such as we need to put you on projects that make sense for you signals that a decision has already been made, and that a reputation for niceness without sharp edges routes people away from the work that leads to tech lead roles. Her remedy is a more demanding view of emotional intelligence: sitting with uncomfortable feedback, saying no kindly, and giving others the hard truth without wrapping it in a bow. She advises readers to stop trying to control the version of themselves in a decision-maker’s head and to control the next data point they supply, such as plainly reporting that a deployment will slip by three days. She suggests auditing the last three meetings for moments of softening and asking directly for growth assignments.
points: Compliments paired with vague reassignment language are not feedback but evidence that a decision has been made, and the only lever left is the next data point you give decision-makers.
Nice is the surface, while emotional intelligence is the load-bearing structure that lets you deliver hard news, say no, and hear feedback you disagree with.
Warmth and candor can coexist in one conversation: promotable people can be warm and still tell you the deployment will miss the deadline.
A practical self-audit is to count how many times in your last three meetings you softened your words to be nice.
quotes: If leadership can give you just compliments but cannot articulate what will get you to the next level, they are not giving you feedback. The decision has already been made.
A sweet reputation plus no sharp edges equals being routed away from business-critical work.
The label gets stacked against you, and your competence discounted. The sweeter you are perceived, the less weight your technical judgment carries.

Real EQ is sitting with your own uncomfortable emotions. That handling is a muscle: learning to sit with feedback you don’t agree with long enough to separate the sting from the signal is where real EQ actually shows up.
Nice is the surface. EQ is the load-bearing structure that goes beyond that and helps tough conversations and business-impact projects land your way.
The people who get promoted can be warm and tell you the deployment will miss the deadline by a few days. Both can exist in the same conversation.
You cannot control the version of you that is already in the decision-maker’s mind. You can control the next data point you give them. That is the only lever.
Audit your last three meetings. When did you soften your words before you said it, to be “nice”? The number is your signal.
